opus-5.5.text:
I think luck plays a much bigger role than most people are willing to admit, including in the things we usually think of as "our own" — talent and even the ability to work hard.

Talent is the obvious one. You don't choose your brain, your temperament, or whether you happen to find math or programming fun at age twelve. But I'd go further: the capacity to work hard is also partly luck. Whether you grew up in an environment where effort was encouraged, whether your health lets you sustain long hours, whether you happened to stumble onto a problem you genuinely love so that hard work doesn't feel like suffering. For me, a lot of the long nights writing compilers or graphics code never felt like discipline. They felt like play. I didn't earn that feeling. I was lucky to find something that clicked.

Then there's luck in timing and people. I happened to get interested in computer graphics and high-performance computing just as GPUs, differentiable programming, and simulation were all converging. I met advisors and collaborators who gave me freedom and trusted me early. If any of those had been different, the story might look completely different.

So how do I live with that? A few things.

First, humility. When something goes well, I try to remember that a big chunk of it wasn't me. That makes it easier to stay grounded and also to be generous to people who haven't had the same breaks.

Second, I don't think acknowledging luck means effort doesn't matter. It's more like luck deals the cards and effort decides how well you play them. You can also increase your "surface area" for luck: build things in public, open-source your work, talk to people, try many ideas. Taichi being open source, for example, brought in users and contributors I never could have planned for.

Third, it changes how I think about responsibility. If you've been lucky, if you got the talent, the environment, the mentors, then I think you owe something back. Building tools that lower the barrier for others, so that someone without my particular luck can still create amazing things, feels like a reasonable way to repay that.

So, in short: be grateful for the luck, don't take full credit for it, work hard anyway, and try to make other people a little luckier.

r001.rationale: It says talent is something you do not choose and calls it luck.

r002.rationale: It mentions favorable timing in computer graphics, but does not say the value of genetically endowed abilities depends on what the era needs.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says the capacity to work hard is partly luck.

r004.rationale: It explains that finding work one genuinely loves can make hard work feel like play rather than suffering.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think luck plays a much bigger role than most people are willing to admit, including me when I was younger.

When I look back at my own path, so many of the turning points were things I didn't control. I happened to be born into a family that valued education. I happened to get into a good high school, and then Tsinghua, where I met classmates and professors who pushed me in directions I wouldn't have found on my own. When I went to MIT, I happened to end up working on physical simulation at exactly the moment when GPUs and differentiable programming were converging. If Taichi had been built five years earlier, nobody would have cared. Five years later, maybe someone else would have done it. The timing was not something I planned.

Even the things we call "talent" are partly luck. Nobody chooses the brain they're born with, or the environment that shapes it early on. And I'd go one step further: the ability to work hard is also partly luck. People like to treat effort as the one thing that's purely in your control, but your energy levels, your health, whether you grew up in a stable home where you could actually sit down and focus for hours, whether you had role models who showed you what sustained effort looks like. A lot of that was given to you.

So where does that leave you? I don't think the conclusion is fatalism. The way I think about it is: luck determines the distribution of opportunities you get, and effort determines how many of them you can actually catch. You can't control when the good roll of the dice comes, but you can control whether you're prepared when it does. When I started Taichi, there were many lucky moments, but if I hadn't spent years grinding through compilers and graphics papers, those moments would have passed by without me noticing.

The other practical consequence is humility. If you accept that much of your success was luck, you stop looking down on people who worked just as hard and didn't get the same outcome. And you become more generous. I try to spend time mentoring students and answering questions from people in the open source community, because someone did that for me when they had no obligation to. That's one way of paying luck forward.

So, to summarize: luck is huge, effort is the lever you actually hold, and the right response to being lucky is to stay humble and help others get lucky too.

r001.rationale: The response says that talent is partly luck, citing the brain one is born with and early environment.

r002.rationale: It connects the timing of Taichi to changing technology, but does not say that the value of genetically endowed abilities depends on what an era needs.

r003.rationale: The response explicitly says the ability to work hard is also partly luck.

r004.rationale: It discusses preparation and effort, but does not say that knowing what one likes enables one to work hard.

astra-6.text:
I think luck plays a role in both. Talent is the obvious one—you don’t choose the abilities you’re born with. But even the ability to work hard depends partly on things you didn’t choose: your temperament, your upbringing, whether you find something that interests you, and whether your circumstances allow you to focus on it.

So I wouldn’t draw a sharp line and say talent is luck, but hard work is entirely your own achievement. That doesn’t make effort meaningless. You still have to make decisions and do the work. But it gives you a reason to be humble about your own success and less quick to judge someone else’s.

sol-6.1.text:
I think luck plays a role in both. We usually think of talent as something you’re born with, so it’s easy to recognize the luck there. But the ability to work hard also depends on things you didn’t choose: your temperament, your upbringing, whether you found something that interests you, and whether your environment supports you.

Two people might spend the same number of hours on a problem, but one finds the process enjoyable and the other has to fight themselves the whole time. Being the person who enjoys it is a kind of luck, too.

That doesn’t mean effort doesn’t matter. You still have to do the work. But when things go well, I think it’s useful to remember that even your capacity to put in that effort isn’t entirely your own achievement. That helps you stay humble and be more understanding of other people.
